summary: This standards-track memo describes using AES in Galois/Counter Mode with IPsec ESP to provide both confidentiality and data origin authentication. It can be implemented efficiently in hardware for very high speeds.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how to use a fast kind of lock that both hides your data and proves it was not changed, in one go.

questions: how to use gcm with ipsec
how does gcm work with esp
what is the nonce format for aes-gcm esp
what icv lengths does aes-gcm esp allow
subtitle: How to use AES in Galois/Counter Mode so IPsec ESP can encrypt and authenticate packets in a single fast pass.

tldr.problem: Counter mode encrypts fast but proves nothing about who sent the data, and the standard authentication algorithms could not keep up with very high data rates.
tldr.mechanism: AES-GCM encrypts and authenticates in one operation. The RFC maps GCM's inputs onto ESP fields: an 8-octet IV, a 4-octet salt from IKE keying material, and an AAD made of the SPI and sequence number.
tldr.outcome: IPsec connections can protect packets with one parallelizable algorithm at 10 gigabit speeds and above, as long as the same nonce and key are never used twice.

today: RFC 4106 is a Proposed Standard from June 2005. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why GCM for ESP
sections.content:
RFC 4106 describes how to use the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) inside the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). The RFC calls the combination AES-GCM-ESP. It provides confidentiality and data origin authentication, and it can be implemented efficiently in hardware at 10 gigabits per second and above.

Counter mode (CTR) is the preferred encryption method for high-speed implementations because it can be pipelined, and RFC 3686 shows how to use it with ESP. But CTR gives no data origin authentication, so ESP CTR needs a separate authentication algorithm, and none of the standard ones could run efficiently at high data rates. GCM solves this by combining CTR mode with a secure, parallelizable and efficient authentication mechanism.

The RFC does not cover how GCM itself works. Those details and the test vectors live in the GCM specification it cites.
sections.plainLanguage: Hiding a message and signing it used to be two slow jobs. GCM does both at once, so the network does not have to slow down.

sections.title: How AES-GCM Is Used
sections.content:
GCM's authenticated encryption takes four inputs: a secret key, an initialization vector (IV), a plaintext and additional authenticated data (AAD). It produces a ciphertext of the same length as the plaintext, plus an authentication tag.

ESP already has its own IV field, so to avoid confusion the RFC calls the AES-GCM IV a nonce. The same nonce and key combination MUST NOT be used more than once, because reuse destroys the security guarantees of the mode. That is hard to guarantee with statically configured keys, so implementations MUST use an automated key management system such as the Internet Key Exchange (IKE).
sections.plainLanguage: The lock needs a fresh, never-used number every time, like a ticket stub you can only use once. A robot that hands out keys automatically makes sure no number repeats.

sections.title: ESP Payload and Nonce
sections.content:
The ESP payload data is an eight-octet IV followed by the ciphertext. The IV MUST be eight octets and MUST NOT repeat for a given key. A counter is the natural choice, but anything that guarantees uniqueness works, such as a linear feedback shift register. The sender can choose its method without coordinating with the receiver.

The plaintext given to GCM is the data described by the Next Header field, followed by the Padding, the Pad Length and the Next Header field. Implementations that do not want to hide the plaintext length SHOULD use the minimum padding, which is less than four octets.

The nonce handed to GCM is built from a four-octet salt followed by the eight-octet IV. The salt is assigned when the security association starts and stays constant for its life. It SHOULD be unpredictable (chosen at random), but need not be secret.
sections.plainLanguage: Each package carries its own one-time number, and the sender and receiver also share a small secret-ish number that never changes. Put them together and you get the number the lock uses.

sections.title: AAD, ICV and Packet Growth
sections.content:
The SPI and the sequence number are sent unencrypted, but they are still protected: they go into the GCM AAD. There are two AAD formats, one with a 32-bit sequence number and one with a 64-bit extended sequence number.

The Integrity Check Value (ICV) is just the GCM authentication tag. Implementations MUST support a 16-octet ICV, MAY support 8 or 12 octets, and MUST NOT support other lengths. A zero-length ICV is deliberately not allowed, because GCM gives no integrity protection at all with a zero-length tag.

The packet grows by the eight-octet IV plus an 8, 12 or 16 octet ICV, plus 10 to 13 octets for the ESP SPI, Sequence Number, Padding, Pad Length and Next Header fields when minimal padding is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Some labels on the outside of the package stay readable, but the lock still checks that nobody changed them. The seal can be a few different sizes, but never zero.

sections.title: IKE Conventions
sections.content:
The keying material (KEYMAT) that IKE produces for each AES-GCM key must be four octets longer than the AES key itself. The extra four octets become the salt. That means 20 octets for a 128-bit key, 28 for a 192-bit key and 36 for a 256-bit key.

For IKE Phase 2, IANA assigned three ESP transform identifiers for AES-GCM with an eight-byte explicit IV, and the Key Length attribute MUST be present with a value of 128, 192 or 256. The RFC does not define AES-GCM for IKE Phase 1; it recommends a Phase 1 cipher at least as strong, such as AES-CBC with the same key size.
sections.plainLanguage: When the two sides agree on a key, they ask for a few extra bytes. The key uses most of them and the leftover four become the shared extra number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
GCM is provably secure against adversaries that can adaptively choose plaintexts, ciphertexts, ICVs and AAD, under standard cryptographic assumptions. Used within its intended parameters, breaking GCM implies breaking the underlying block cipher.

The most important rule is that the IV never repeats for a given key. IKE establishes separate keys for the two traffic flows. If a mechanism establishes only one key shared by both directions, the peers could pick the same IVs, so ESP implementations that use one key in both directions MUST ensure the two peers assign different salt values.

Security also decreases slightly with each message, so implementations MUST generate a fresh key before encrypting 2^64 blocks with a given key. That limit cannot be reached with 32-bit sequence numbers. Smaller ICVs are more open to forgery, so implementations SHOULD use as large an ICV as reasonable.
sections.plainLanguage: The big rule is never to reuse a one-time number. Change the key before it has been used too much, and prefer the longer seal because it is harder to fake.

sections.title: Design Rationale
sections.content:
The design copies the AES-CCM ESP and AES-CTR ESP mechanisms as closely as reasonable, while keeping implementations simple and efficient in both hardware and software.

The main difference from CCM is nonce size. CCM ESP needs an 11-octet nonce, while GCM ESP uses a 12-octet nonce because GCM is specially optimized for that length. Other lengths would add complexity and delay, especially in hardware. The extra octet goes into a larger salt.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock works fastest with one particular size of number, so the designers picked that size and used the spare byte to make the shared part bigger.

fields.name: Salt
fields.desc: Four octets fixed for the life of the security association.

fields.name: Initialization Vector
fields.desc: Eight octets that must not repeat for a given key.
